title: DLQ Retry Strategies and Backoff
description: Learn retry patterns including exponential backoff, fixed delay, and circuit breakers to handle transient failures without overwhelming downstream services.

data.text: Not every failure is permanent. Network blips, temporary outages, and rate limits often clear up on their own. Retry strategies let your system attempt processing again without human intervention, while backoff schedules prevent retries from hammering a struggling service.

data.title: Retry Strategies
items: Immediate retry: try again right away; useful for rare, transient glitches but risks tight retry loops
Fixed delay retry: wait a constant interval between attempts; simple and predictable
Exponential backoff: double the wait time after each failure (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s); reduces load on recovering services
Exponential backoff with jitter: add randomness to avoid thundering herd when many clients retry simultaneously
Circuit breaker: stop sending requests after repeated failures and open the circuit for a cooldown period

data.text: Exponential backoff with jitter is the most robust default. Jitter prevents synchronized retries that can create sudden traffic spikes. A typical pattern uses a base delay of 1 second, caps the delay at 60 seconds, and adds up to 1 second of randomness.

data.caption: Exponential backoff retry flow
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Receive Message] --> B[Attempt Processing]
    B -->|Success| C[Delete / Ack]
    B -->|Transient Failure| D{Retry Count < Max?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Wait: 2^n + jitter]
    E --> B
    D -->|No| F[Send to DLQ]

data.title: Retry Storms
data.text: Without jitter, many failed messages retry at the same time, creating a traffic spike that can worsen the outage. Always add randomness to your delay.

items.question: Should I retry every failure?
items.answer: No. Retry only transient errors like network timeouts or 503 responses. Permanent errors such as 400 Bad Request or validation failures should go straight to the DLQ.

items.question: What is a good max retry count?
items.answer: Three to five retries is typical. More retries delay detection of persistent problems and increase end-to-end latency.

items.question: How does jitter prevent retry storms?
items.answer: Jitter spreads retry attempts across a time window instead of bunching them together. This keeps traffic smooth when many messages fail at once.
